After your shift you lie in the barracks like any tired man, and at the second bell you slip out with your father's axe across your back. The torch goes to the east coal shed, the one farthest from the third gate's stair. The dry slack catches and roars up orange against the dark, and you are already crouching in the black shadow beside the Counting House when the shouting starts.

He's not here tonight." "Then who's to say, with the move at dawn?" "The move was the twentieth." "The Foreman moved it up. Tomorrow's dawn, the whole lot, the book and the brats together." They bolt for the fire.

So the Foreman is not in the ledger-house tonight, and the master ledger is going down the mountain at dawn.

You go in fast and low. The scribe is a thin goblin with ink on his chin, and he has half risen when you take him by the collar. You bellow that he'll live if he sits quiet, but your grip is wrong, and he twists like an eel and gets out one thin, piercing yelp before you jam the gag in his mouth. Outside, a boot scrapes. One of the guards has turned back toward the door.

The copy sits on the shelf behind the desk, a thick book bound in grey leather, the lamp burning an arm's length from it. The scribe is bound but thrashing. The guard's shadow is on the threshold.

It is just after ten at night. What does Korvash do?

entries.text: notebook: updated Break the Foreman's Ledger

You stand your post until the shift bell and go back up to the barracks like any other tired man. Pip's snore is steady under his cap. At the second night bell you ease out again, and this time your father's greataxe rides on your back and a torch from your pack is in your fist. Tonight you do not leave Dargan's axe behind.

The east coal shed is the farthest from the third gate's stair. You light the torch from your tinderbox in the lee of its wall and set it to the dry slack, and the coal catches with a hungry orange crawl. You are back in the shadow beside the Counting House before the first shout goes up.

It goes as you hoped, but only half of it. One of the door guards bolts for the fire, bellowing for water. The other does not. He stays by the lamp-lit door with his head tilted toward the dark where you crouch. Your breath, or the creak of the axe-strap, or the shape of a dragonborn against the glow. He draws his sword with a slow rasp.

"Who's there?" he calls, low, and takes a step in your direction. Behind him, through the barred window, the night scribe is half out of his stool, quill in hand. The coal shed roars behind you, and horns are starting up along the walls.

The guard is fifteen feet away and between you and the door. The ledger's lamp burns behind him. Time is going, and every second of it makes the road to the third gate harder. It is ten at night.

What does Korvash do?

input.add_to_description: Day 18, ~10:10 PM: Korvash fired the east coal shed (alarm of fire on the lower wall), the two Counting House door guards ran to it, he bound and gagged the night scribe and burned the COPY ledger in the lamp. The copy is ash. Smoke and a fire bell are rousing the lower camp; the Tally-sworn on the third gate stair will have seen the glow. Tessa's second bell window at the wash-house door is now at risk.

entries.text: notebook: updated Break the Foreman's Ledger

You wait until the barracks have gone quiet, then ease out at the second bell with the greataxe on your back, your father's sash swinging against your shoulder blade. Nobody sees you go. The cold is sharp, the smelters glow red against the clouds, and you keep to the lee of the buildings as if you had been born in their shadow.

The east coal shed catches faster than you hoped. The torch goes into the heap, the dust takes it, and in moments a bright, ugly flame is climbing the planks. You are across the yard and flat against the Counting House wall before the first shout goes up from the lower wall: "Fire! Fire in the coal!" The fire bell starts clanging. Both door guards run past you close enough to touch, cursing, and neither looks left.

You go in low and fast. The night scribe is a thin hobgoblin with ink on his chin, half out of his stool, and you take him by the collar and give him the full bellow of your lungs at an inch's distance: he lives if he sits quiet, and he doesn't if he doesn't. He goes grey and sits so quiet that he nearly stops breathing. His own sash ties his wrists, and his own sleeve is the gag. The copy of the ledger is on the shelf behind the desk, a fat book bound in black leather. It feeds the lamp a page at a time, then all at once. When it is only curling ash on the desk, you drop the lamp's oil on the rest and walk out.

That is the first book. It is just after ten.

The yard is full of smoke and shouting now, with buckets passing along a line and the lower wall's torches all turned toward the glow. But higher up the slope, at the third gate, a different alarm is stirring. Torches are moving along the ledger-house parapet. Someone up there has seen the glow and woken, and the stair guards are looking down.

The drain-stair is at the far side of the slope, the sluice path runs through the dark, and the wash-house door will open at the second bell, which has just rung. What does Korvash do?

entries.text: notebook: updated Gorrak Vael

You get them up, and they come. The ford is a bright cold rattle behind you, and then there is only the high road, rutted and pale, running south between brown slopes. You carry two small ones in turn, one on each arm over the shield, and when a girl's legs give out near noon she rides your back with her chin on your helm-less horns and falls asleep. Ninna keeps the count at every halt. It never comes up short. Behind you the grey shape on the ridge falls farther back, then drops from sight.

Tessa goes ahead, hooded and quick, a rust-colored scrap that is soon out of sight over the rises. She is gone for hours. You do not like it.

A little after two in the afternoon she comes back at a trot, from the south, and drops into step beside you without breath to spare. "Twenty of them," she says in Draconic. "Hobgoblins, mail and shields, walking in column, two miles on. Gorrak at the front in the tin mask, with the rod in his belt. They aren't running and no one's got a spear couched. They're just coming. They'll meet us before the next bend in the road, in an hour, no more."

She looks back at the long straggling line of children, at the ridge, at you. "The grey cloaks behind, Vael ahead. If he means to turn us back, this is the place. If he means to deal, it's still the place. I'll stay with the little ones, or I'll stand by you. You say."

You are at 5 hit points, with a longsword, a shield, your breath back in your chest, and your rage still cold. It is a little after two in the afternoon. What does Korvash do?

You get them up with the old loudness pitched low, and the column crosses the stream in a chain of hands, the tallest boys wading the deep channel with the little ones on their shoulders. Nobody falls in, and nobody complains. Then it's the high road, a rutted track of grey gravel running south between the hills.

Tessa goes ahead, hood up, quick and silent as a lizard on a wall. You take the rear with the shield on your arm, and the children plod on in their chains of ten, Ninna calling the count at every rest. Twice a small one goes down from weariness and rides a while on your back. Behind you, always the same distance, a grey shape keeps pace along the ridgeline.

The day wears on to mid-afternoon. At about half past three, Tessa comes trotting back along the verge and drops into step beside you, breathing hard.

She looks at you. "It's Vael, Kor. He rode hard. They'll be on us within the hour, and they haven't seen us yet."

The road here runs in a shallow bowl between two low hills, with a dry stone wall along one side and a cluster of boulders on the other. The children are strung out behind you in the open. You are at 5 hit points, your breath weapon is ready, and Rage is spent.

line:
The rest is done and every hour nearer Greyshaft's hounds is an hour wasted, so I get the column on its feet. "Up, little ones, we cross here and take the high road home, and anyone too tired rides on my back."

I send Tessa ahead along the road hooded and quick to scout for Vael's column, and I walk the rear with the shield on my arm and my breath weapon ready, so that if Gorrak arrives it's on the open road with the children well behind me.

input.add_to_description: Day 19 ~2 PM: came up the high road early with Sergeant Ushk and about a dozen Iron Tallies, halting at a shallow ford ahead of Korvash's column. Has not yet drawn steel; waiting for Korvash to come to him.

entries.text: notebook: updated Gorrak Vael

You get them up and moving, and the column crosses the stream in a long line, big children carrying little ones, your shield on your arm and the rear in your charge. Twice you stop to let the smallest drink. Twice the grey shape on the ridge stops when you do. Ninna keeps the count aloud, and it is never wrong.

Tessa goes ahead hooded and quick, a rust-red shadow along the verge. She is gone most of the morning. The sun climbs, the road runs on between stone walls and bare larches, and by early afternoon the children have gone quiet with weariness.

It is ten past two when she comes back at a run, dropping to a walk when she sees the column. "A mile on," she says, low, in Draconic. "Where the road goes down to a shallow ford. Soldiers. A dozen, maybe more, in a line across the road, and Ushk is with them. In the middle, the tin mask." She swallows. "They aren't hiding, Kor. They've stacked their spears and are sitting down. He's waiting for you."

You are at 5 hit points, with your breath weapon back, no rage, a longsword and a shield. Ninety-four children are strung out behind you on an open road, and the grey scouts are still on the ridge. The ford is a mile off.
